The symptoms became more disabling and 3 years before admission she discontinued work. Diazepam was effective but required gradually increasing doses. Carbamazepine lessened her pain but not the stiffness, baclofen was transiently effective in reducing severe stiffness, and lorazepam and clonazepam were less effective than diazepam. Immunomodulating therapies had not been tried.

extractions.quote: On initial examination the patient was awake and able to provide a detailed history. She was lying in bed with legs in stiff extensor posture, arms in modified flexor posture, spine hyperlordotic, and muscles of the abdomen hard. The plantar response was extensor; sensation and coordination were intact. Sudden noise provoked spasm and increased stiffness. Administration of IV diazepam produced drowsiness and relief of stiffness such that the patient attained a seated posture and propelled a wheelchair. EMG showed involuntary continuous motor unit activity of agonist–antagonist muscle groups consistent with SPS. The serum was negative for antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase, amphiphysin, and gephyrin. MRI of the brain and spinal cord showed increased lumbar lordosis but were otherwise normal.

Daily administration of tiagabine 4 mg was introduced during hospitalization. Initially the diazepam dose was 60 mg daily and clonazepam was 4.5 mg daily. Seven days after initiation of tiagabine, diazepam was tapered by 10 mg every 3 days to a dose of 10 mg daily. Over the subsequent 3 months tiagabine was titrated to 6 mg daily; diazepam ranged from 5 to 15 mg daily. At her first follow-up visit the patient demonstrated markedly reduced tone including face, arms, and legs. The patient had difficulty standing because she was used to locking her knees to ambulate and could not do so; strength in the lower extremities was mildly decreased. After 2 months of rehabilitation she was able to walk with bilateral cane support.
